notes: Simulation models (gbm, reservoir) use drivers only (weather, soil wetness, MODIS cover, CDL, observed streamflow) - no lagged nitrate. Persistence baselines use nitrate observed 7/14 days earlier, so they are forecasts with information the simulation models do not get.
Metrics are computed on concentration (mg/L) over days with an observation and a prediction.
gbm p10/p90 are conformalized (CQR) with leave-one-year-out residuals from 2016-2022.
Cover features are causal (as-of MODIS composites; see notes/model.md).

05482000.name: Des Moines River at 2nd Ave, Des Moines

v2.label: post-hoc (v2 designed after seeing the v1 2025 miss)
v2.what: v1 plus a causal nitrogen carry-over store (prior seasons' rain and drought), designed after seeing the v1 2025 miss

lines: Fair test: the first version of the model (v1) learned from 2016-2022 and was scored on 2023-2025, years it never saw. It captures about 62% of the day-to-day ups and downs of nitrate at the Raccoon River gauge at Van Meter, upstream of the intake (NSE 0.62) and 56% at the Des Moines River (NSE 0.56), against 0.30 and 0.27 for 'the usual level for that date'.

It never sees measured nitrate, only NASA weather and soil wetness, satellite cover, crops and river flow. Persistence ('same as 7 days ago') scores higher (0.77), but it needs last week's measurement, so it is a forecast, not an explanation.

Honest miss: in 2025 the Raccoon ran above 10 mg/L on 115 measured days; the v1 model's middle estimate gave 6, although its upper 8-in-10 bound was above 10 mg/L on 121 measured days (plausible, not expected). At the Des Moines River: 105 measured vs 10 modelled.

Why: from early 2025 the rivers carried about 1.7x (Raccoon) and 2.1x (Des Moines) the nitrate that that year's weather, wet soil and bare ground explain, in every season and at low and high flow. Years after droughts run high (2022 and 2024 too), consistent with one hypothesis, nitrate left in soils and groundwater after the 2020-2023 drought (not proven: 2023 ran low right after the 2022 drought; fertilizer, groundwater lag or a rain-data shift could also contribute), a slow store the model has no input for. The 2025 data are USGS-approved, so it is not a sensor artifact.

Raccoon: a second version (v2) adds a nitrogen carry-over store for the years after a drought. It was built after seeing the 2025 miss, so its 2023-2025 score is not a clean test. 2025 days above 10 mg/L: measured 115, v2 83, v1 6. Pre-registered blind check on 2013 (the flush after the 2012 drought, held out): measured 92 days above 10, v2 81, v1 features 80. The chart shows v2 here (display rule fixed before any v2 2026 metric was computed; v1's 2026 miss was already known).

Des Moines: a second version (v2) adds a nitrogen carry-over store for the years after a drought. It was built after seeing the 2025 miss, so its 2023-2025 score is not a clean test. 2025 days above 10 mg/L: measured 105, v2 10, v1 10. The chart shows v2 here (display rule fixed before any v2 2026 metric was computed; v1's 2026 miss was already known).

So the app uses the model for what it does well: RELATIVE what-if changes (less bare soil), applied to the measured river, never its absolute 2025 level. Near-term levels come from the 14-day outlook, which starts from the latest measurement.
The 8-in-10 band held the measured value on 66% of test days (it should be 80%): ranges are somewhat too narrow in new conditions.
14-day outlook: on 2023-2025 it beat 'no change' by 20% at one week and 25% at two weeks (squared error, Raccoon). It uses no weather forecast, so a big storm can push nitrate outside its range.

Removal-plant proxy (the utility's rules are not public): 'plant runs when the 7-day mean of the average of the two rivers' measured nitrate exceeds 10.2 mg/L'. Fitted to 2025 (106 proxy days vs 112 reported); tested on 2026 without refitting: 157 vs 193 days (daily agreement F1 0.897).
